findings.quote: tiny particles that carry electric charge, the thing that moves through the wires when the torch is on
findings.what: Charge is explained only as 'the thing that moves', which is circular. She is left with no idea what charge is beyond a name.

findings.quote: The bigger current is in the wire with more charge passing each second. Which wire has the bigger current?
findings.what: The hint hands her the rule that decides the answer and then asks the same question, so nothing is left to think about.

findings.quote: Start with the charge: how many coulombs pass the point each second in this wire?
findings.what: The hint asks a different question whose answer (3) is printed in the question itself. If she types 3 she is marked right for the amperes without having linked coulombs per second to amperes.

findings.quote: each coulomb a second makes one ampere
findings.what: Awkward wording used in every branch. 'One coulomb each second is one ampere, so 3 coulombs each second is 3 amperes' would be clearer.

findings.what: She has just been told 'The circuit has two ammeters in the same loop' and has used that circuit, so 'In the loop' is not a prediction. The answer was shown before the question.

findings.quote: 60 C of charge flows through a potential difference of 6 V. How much energy is transferred, in joules (J)?
findings.what: As scripted this is identical to the 7.10 practice question, so it tests memory of 360, not the method. If the question really is new each time this may not arise.

findings.quote: A wire is kept at a constant temperature. What happens to its resistance if you use a longer piece?
findings.what: The same wire-length question is asked at 3.8, 3.15, 4.10 and 8.6, and 'what does a straight line through the origin show' at 4.9, 5.13, 6.2 and 8.3. Some returning is good, but four times each will feel like the lesson repeating itself.

overall: Not quite as it is, though key points 1 and 2 are close: the physics is sound and the switch, two-ammeter, add-a-cell and resistor predictions are well built. Before she uses those two I would fix the second ammeter 'prediction' (already answered on screen), the empty description of a resistor, the run of five vocabulary messages with no picture of a voltmeter, and the misplaced rearrangement in 2.15. I would also teach I = V ÷ R, because the quiz asks for it. The later key points need more work: the graph steps (4.3, 5.6, 5.9) are scripted with a circuit that has no controls, both practicals are all telling, resistors 'in series or in parallel' is never explained, and several hints give the answer away or do not match the buttons.
